job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Emeka Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Emeka, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my little brother in Kingsford, and the bathroom queue is part of my routine. My dad drives a taxi and my mum cleans offices before dawn, so the flat is quiet by nine. I check my application tracker, which is a spreadsheet with colour codes, and send about six applications to banks, insurers and a couple of energy firms. In the afternoon I deliver groceries on a scooter three days a week, which covers my phone and loan payment. I studied economics and passed, no internship, and I've had two final-round interviews and no offer in five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's balanced: some use, some hype, and not the end of the world either way. I'd tell friends to use it when it saves time and ignore it when it doesn't. I don't post much online, so mostly I'd just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, same worries as now. I'm a pass-degree graduate with no internship and a loan, applying to places that get hundreds of applicants for each role. AI doesn't change that, and it might make the filtering stricter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the tracker going, aim for eight applications a week and ask my old professor for a reference. I'd keep the delivery work to hold my cash, and practise case-study interviews with my cousin who works at an insurer. Once I get a job, I'd put a third of my pay straight against the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, not great. It feels like being a number in the middle of a queue, but I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your tracker has colour codes. What does it say about where you stand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Green means interview, yellow means waiting, and red means no reply for four weeks. I've got two greens that turned red and a lot of yellow. It tells me I'm good enough to get seen, not good enough to be picked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents make of the job hunt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They say keep going, we believe in you. My dad has driven strangers for thirty years and thinks everything works out if you show up. My mum worries quietly, and she keeps slipping money into my jar for the scooter petrol.

I'd tell friends to use it when it saves **time**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real shift and we should be honest about it. I'd tell friends who are job hunting to learn the tools, and I'd say employers should keep hiring juniors, not just rely on software. I'd say it plainly, without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it worries me. Entry roles in banks and insurers are claims checking, data entry and basic reporting, which software takes first. A friend in an insurer says they already hired fewer juniors this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn a data tool properly, probably spreadsheets with scripts and a basic reporting package, through an online course in the evenings. I'd start using AI to summarise reports in my interview prep, and aim for roles that mix numbers and clients, like relationship support. I'd cut my delivery hours only if I got a job, and stretch my savings meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned but not frozen. There's a plan to try, so it's more annoying than scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the bank and insurance entry roles do you think shrinks first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claims checking and reconciliation. Those are rule-based, and a computer does them faster. Roles with client contact, like explaining a policy, will probably last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the insurers stop hiring graduates altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try utilities and local government, because they hire in slow cycles. If those fail, I'd consider an accountancy trainee scheme at a small firm, which is not my dream but pays. I'd also think about moving to a bigger city, though I hate leaving my family.

say: I'd say it's a real **shift** and employers should keep hiring juniors, said plainly.
I'd tell job-hunting friends to learn the **tools**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need clear plans from the government within weeks, like income support and retraining. I'd tell friends to keep a calm head, and I'd share any local help I find. I'm not one to shout, but I'd speak up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be rattled. Economics and finance are thinking work, and the card says that goes first by 2028. I'd be twenty-five with a thin CV and a loan, and my parents' jobs are not exactly safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work more delivery shifts, since that's hands-on and robots take longer. I'd cut everything extra, move my small savings to the safest account, and ask my dad about the taxi drivers' association for help and advice. I'd also apply to the trades-adjacent jobs in finance, like payroll at a building firm, where people still need to be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and sleepless. Two years is not a long time to be wrong about anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first month after the announcement look like in your house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say we'll manage, my mum would say nothing and count the bills. We'd probably sit at the table, put every cost on paper, and cut three things. I'd probably give up the phone upgrade and the gym first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paying the minimum and nothing extra, because a cash cushion matters more than interest at that moment. I'd check whether the loan repayments pause when income falls.

I'd tell friends to keep a calm head and share local **help**.

My parents' jobs are not **safe** either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and it should come with action: retraining funds, support for people who lose work and clear rules. I'd tell friends to start learning now. I'd stay level-headed online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel manageable worry. If I land a job in the next year, I'd have four years of experience and a decent record. Still, I'd keep a plan B ready, because the thinking work is the first to be taken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job at an insurer, a bank or anywhere with finance work, and ask to rotate through teams. I'd learn the AI tools as part of the work, then use evenings for a certification, maybe in risk or compliance. I'd put a third of my pay toward my loan and a third in savings, so I'd have room if things shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned but steady. It's a long road with some light on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two would not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is crisis mode. Five years is one hard push and then a period of adjustment. I'd rather have the second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you split your attention between a job and learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe forty percent learning in work hours, if a firm allows it, and some in the evenings. I'd also keep delivery shifts on Saturday for cash and a reality check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if we use it, so let's plan training, savings and rules now. I'd tell friends not to freeze. I'd keep it practical and calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel mostly steady. I could build a career in finance, change direction if needed and even afford something small, like a flat deposit. I'd still pay attention, because ten years goes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job, stay two to three years, then specialise in something that needs judgement, like credit risk or advice. I'd keep learning tools as they appear. I'd save for a deposit and help my parents with their bills when I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, even a bit hopeful. It's like a long hill I can see the top of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make it feel like a normal career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost, but with a question mark over how roles change in year seven or eight. I'd keep a list of skills that a machine can't do easily, like talking to a worried client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your little brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn to work with people and with tools, and not to count on a single career. He's fifteen and loves football, so I'd also tell him to keep that, because there's more to life than jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. My parents' jobs and mine would all be hit before anyone has a plan. What would help is a clear job route for new graduates, income support while we retrain, and a government that tells the truth early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that we're not lazy and we're not entitled. We're applying, working and paying, and a bit of honesty about how few entry jobs there are would help.

His parents' work as a taxi driver and an office cleaner adds a household worry.
